docs.abstract: A biography of Joan Didion — Californian, New Yorker, American.
docs.snippet: A biography of Joan Didion — Californian, New Yorker, American.
docs.lead_paragraph: In a spiky little essay on the painter Georgia O’Keeffe, Joan Didion writes ­coded instructions for would-be biographers. “Where I was born and where and how I have lived is unimportant,” she quotes ­O’Keeffe. “It is what I have done with where I have been that should be of interest.” In other words, study the particulars of the paintings, not the particulars of the life. In the next sentence, however, Didion tells the story of her 7-year-old daughter, who, on seeing one of O’Keeffe’s sublime “Sky Above Clouds” paintings in the Art Institute of Chicago, runs toward it and whispers: “Who drew it? . . . I need to talk to her.” The longing to corroborate one’s own feelings with the facts of an artist’s life — the assumption “that the glory she saw in the work reflected a glory in its maker” — is a primal one, Didion suggests. But there is a paradox inherent in the encounter with art: Even as it may touch us acutely, it is essentially mysterious. It carries only a trace of its maker, and this is style. “Style is character,” Didion declares, throwing down the gauntlet: Find me if you can.

headline.main: ‘The Last Love Song,’ a Biography of Joan Didion
headline.print_headline: Coast to Coast

docs.abstract: A playful novel shaped by inventive collaborations.
docs.snippet: A playful novel shaped by inventive collaborations.
docs.lead_paragraph: On its not-so-placid surface, Valeria Luiselli’s second novel is the tale of a guy named Gustavo (Highway) Sánchez Sánchez, who auctions off his old teeth, claiming they are from the mouths of Plato, Montaigne, Virginia Woolf and Borges, among others. Then he takes his profits and buys a set of teeth that supposedly belonged to Marilyn Monroe, implanting them in his own mouth. After that, things go well for a while until Highway’s son, Siddhartha, knocks him out and steals Monroe’s teeth, leaving his dad chopperless. Eventually Highway runs into a man named Voragine (an abyss?) who helps him, and who later appears to be the person telling this story. Along the way, the names of Proust, Unamuno, Foucault, Walser, Cortázar and Raymond Roussel burst out of random paragraphs like startled grouse.

headline.main: ‘The Story of My Teeth,’ by Valeria Luiselli

docs.abstract: Despite his surprisingly straightforward approach to acting, the man who will soon play both Macbeth and Steve Jobs is full of contradictions. On the road with film’s magnetic outsider.
docs.snippet: Despite his surprisingly straightforward approach to acting, the man who will soon play both Macbeth and Steve Jobs is full of contradictions. On the road with film’s magnetic outsider.
docs.lead_paragraph: “I HAD ALREADY been turned down by two drama schools,” Michael Fassbender was explaining over breakfast in one of those New York hotel restaurants where beautiful people add wheatgrass to their smoothies. That rejection at 19 led him to London to try his luck auditioning for the Drama Centre there. He had prepared an Iago monologue, had gone over it hundreds of times, but he was still nervous. He had been replaying the words of a director from one of the other drama schools, who had told him that he could recognize an actor from the way he enters a room. ‘‘I still hate that,’’ said Fassbender. Before the audition, he was trying to get the director’s words out of his mind. ‘‘I went to the urinal, and as I was pissing, I saw that someone had written ‘Hi, Cookie!’ on the wall. Those words were staring at me, as I stood there. I had just finished playing the Cook in a production of ‘Mother Courage,’ and I had done it with a Scottish accent. Cook; cookie. ‘I’ll do the Iago monologue in a Scottish accent,’ I decided, even though that wasn’t how I had prepared it.’’ After the audition, Fassbender was asked why he’d chosen that accent, to which he answered something about it being a way to bring mischief into the piece, which seemed true enough. ‘‘It’s funny. I haven’t thought about that for years and years. I’m not saying what I saw was a sign or anything. But maybe I did sort of take it that way, and that helped me.’’

headline.main: Michael Fassbender, Nobody’s Fool
headline.print_headline: Nobody’s Fool

docs.abstract: It would seem that the demise of the mechanical watch would be fast approaching, but high-end timepieces are doing just fine.
docs.snippet: It would seem that the demise of the mechanical watch would be fast approaching, but high-end timepieces are doing just fine.
docs.lead_paragraph: With the rise of digital devices that tell time, track your steps and even pay the dinner bill, it would seem that the demise of the mechanical watch would be fast approaching. But in fact, high-end timepieces are doing just fine. Last year, Switzerland exported a record $24.3 billion worth of them (which says nothing of the equally booming vintage business). And while the Apple watch, which launched in April and sold an estimated 2.5 million units in its first quarter, is likely to affect those numbers, most traditional producers are taking their smart competition in stride. After all, they survived the ravages of the 1970s, when quartz technology made 60,000 watchmakers obsolete. Indeed, the Swiss are in the midst of a horological renaissance in which dedicated collectors wait years — and pay millions — for timepieces that make up for their lack of digital functionality with analog elegance and a promise: Given regular servicing, they’ll run in perpetuity.

headline.main: The Complicated World of Luxury Watches

docs.snippet: The University of Cincinnati officer, Raymond Tensing, “was not justified in using deadly force” in a July traffic stop, a university consultant said.
docs.lead_paragraph: A University of Cincinnati police officer “was not justified in using deadly force” in a July 19 traffic stop in which he fatally shot a driver, a consultant hired by the university reported Friday. The security firm Kroll reported that video shot by Officer Raymond Tensing’s body camera contradicts his central claim, that his arm was caught in Samuel DuBose’s car, and he was being dragged. It said Officer Tensing, who has been charged with murder, appeared to have his arm free, and the car had not moved, or had barely moved, when he fired at Mr. DuBose. Calling the shooting “entirely preventable,” the report faulted both men for needlessly escalating the situation before that point — Mr. DuBose by disobeying the officer’s instructions and restarting his car, as if to drive off. Kroll also said the university police were unsuited to street-level policing, especially off campus, and should consider narrowing their mission.

headline.main: Ohio: Report Says Killing by Officer Was Preventable

docs.lead_paragraph: Guests were told to bring government-issued identification to the Givenchy show, which was held last night on Manhattan’s Pier 26 — an enormous space jutting into the Hudson River and in the shadow of the Freedom Tower. They were greeted by a set of recycled industrial materials crafted into giant pillars where performance artists (under the direction of Marina Abramovic) stood. Atop one pillar, a couple moved in different stages of embrace; under another, a woman in a white dress shirt stood quietly under a running shower. A monk chanted through the loudspeakers. “The 11th of September is the most sad day in recent American history,” wrote Abramovic in her notes for the show. “As the artistic director, I want to create something respectful and humble.”

headline.main: Givenchy’s Giant New York Spectacle

docs.lead_paragraph: Over the years, I have had the good fortune to teach a lot of graduate students, mostly in philosophy, and have noticed a recurring fact. Behind every new graduate student stands an undergraduate teacher. This is someone who opened the student’s eyes and ears to the possibility of the life of the mind that they had perhaps imagined but scarcely believed was within their reach. Someone who, through the force of their example, animated a desire to read more, study more and know more. Someone in whom the student heard something fascinating or funny or just downright strange. Someone who heard something significant in what the student said in a way that gave them confidence and self-belief. Such teachers are the often unknown and usually unacknowledged (and underpaid) heroes of the world of higher education.

docs.abstract: In honor of his tenth anniversary in fashion, the designer threw a fete that included dancers on poles and fake currency baring his likeness.
docs.snippet: In honor of his tenth anniversary in fashion, the designer threw a fete that included dancers on poles and fake currency baring his likeness.
docs.lead_paragraph: As soon as the lights had dimmed on Alexander Wang’s 10th-anniversary show on Pier 94 last night, a wall pulled back to reveal a party: a cavernous space filled with ice luges, pink-neon lights and six acrobatic dancers gyrating up and down poles. The room was littered with fake currency emblazoned with Wang’s likeness — $10 bills bearing the unofficial signature of Treasurer “Spend Lyka Dem” in honor of his clothing line’s first decade in business. The currency was scattered on the concrete of a roped-off VIP section, where Lady Gaga, Kanye West, Nicki Minaj, Mary J. Blige, Kylie Jenner, Tyga, Miguel, the Weeknd and the Fat Jew mingled and danced on banquettes. Waitstaff from Hooters served chicken wings and sliders while an ice sculpture spelled “Wang10.” A DJ mixed together an irregular-heartbeat-inducing medley that included Missy Elliott’s “Lose Control,” David Banner’s “Play” — until early in the morning, Tinashe, Lil Wayne and Ludacris took the stage for a surprise set.

headline.main: Scenes From Alexander Wang’s All-Night Rager

docs.abstract: This revival of a work choreographed by Lucinda Childs and scored by John Adams, with a set by Frank Gehry, mines a breathtaking spectrum of kaleidoscopic patterns.
docs.snippet: This revival of a work choreographed by Lucinda Childs and scored by John Adams, with a set by Frank Gehry, mines a breathtaking spectrum of kaleidoscopic patterns.
docs.lead_paragraph: In the midst of an extensive European tour, “Available Light,” a 1983 collaboration among the choreographer Lucinda Childs, the composer John Adams and the architect Frank Gehry, made an American stop over the weekend. Presented by FringeArts in Philadelphia as part of the 2015 Fringe Festival, the work took over the Drexel University Armory, a space vast enough to accommodate its grand if minimalist proportions. Ms. Childs was among the revolutionaries of Judson Dance Theater in the 1960s, and like some of her fellow postmodernists she has found a more ardent audience — and more funding, presumably — in Europe than in the United States. But as the writer Suzanne Carbonneau notes in a program essay, Philadelphia has been good to her, with the Pew Center for Arts & Heritage supporting the reconstruction of her early works and giving them a handsome online platform, the exemplary archival project “A Steady Pulse: Restaging Lucinda Childs, 1963-78.” You can enjoy that from anywhere.

headline.main: Review: ‘Available Light’ Takes Over an Armory at Philadelphia’s Fringe Festival
headline.print_headline: A Blizzard of Kaleidoscopic Fragments Click Into Place

docs.abstract: First an ichneumonid wasp lays an egg on an orb weaver spider. The larva essentially turns the spider into a zombie, uses its web and eats the spider.
docs.snippet: First an ichneumonid wasp lays an egg on an orb weaver spider. The larva essentially turns the spider into a zombie, uses its web and eats the spider.
docs.lead_paragraph: If spiders had nightmares, the larvae of ichneumonid wasps would have to star in them. The wasp lays an egg on the back of an orb weaver spider, where it grows fat and bossy, and occupies itself with turning the spider into a zombie. As Keizo Takasuka and his colleagues point out in The Journal of Experimental Biology, this is a classic case of “host manipulation.” Using more colorful language, he described the larva turning the spider into a “drugged navvy.”

headline.main: A Wasp That Turns a Spider Into the Walking Dead

docs.lead_paragraph: In all the fanfare surrounding the Supreme Court’s end-of-term rulings this past June, a little-noticed passage in an opinion by Justice Stephen Breyer quietly revisited a debate that has roiled American law for nearly two decades. Dissenting on the final day of the term from a decision to uphold Oklahoma’s new lethal injection protocol, Breyer (joined by Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg) observed that 137 countries — a full 70 percent of member states in the United Nations — have abolished the death penalty either formally or in practice. Breyer noted further that in 2013 the United States was one of only 22 countries in the world to carry out any executions at all.

headline.main: Stephen Breyer’s ‘The Court and the World’

The bright spots, spangled across the bottom of the Occator crater, may be ice formed by water leaking from below, or perhaps salt left after the water evaporated. Mission scientists also produced a 3-D topographic map of the crater, finding that in places, the rim rises almost vertically for one mile.

docs.lead_paragraph: 10:55 A.M. (Encore) SAVING MR. BANKS (2013) Tom Hanks stars as Walt Disney in this Disney movie directed by John Lee Hancock about the making of “Mary Poppins,” which at the time of its creation in the early 1960s was the most expensive live-action film the studio had produced. It eventually became one of the most beloved, too, and one of the biggest moneymakers. Emma Thompson is the author P. L. Travers, who conjured the magical nanny and is something of a crank. “I won’t have her turned into one of your silly cartoons,” she says of her creation, lips pursed. There’s a back story, too, in which Travers is a little girl (Annie Rose Buckley) in a dusty Australian town, where her hopelessly alcoholic father (Colin Farrell) can barely hold on to his bank job. Writing in The New York Times, A. O. Scott called this movie “part of the Disney brand, of course: fun for everyone, with a spoonful of therapeutic medicine to help the sugar seem nutritious.” (Image: From left, Lily Bigham, Ms. Buckley, Ruth Wilson and Mr. Farrell.)

docs.lead_paragraph: Four years ago, real estate dictated fate for friends Kyle Clairmont Jacques, 27, and Alexander Johns, 28, when a search for an affordable joint studio turned into the opening of Signal — an independently minded art gallery in Bushwick, Brooklyn. “Four or five years ago, everything around here felt slapdash. Sometime during our search for a space, it became very clear that we could present things in this area at a level that was more professional and respectful,” says Clairmont Jacques, an artist-turned-designer who has recently added gallerist to his résumé. “There was nowhere showing art that fit in with the mature contemporary discourse that was happening elsewhere in the city.” Opportunity came in the form of a vaulted industrial space that had been previously used for rug storage, and the duo seized the moment — transforming the warehouse into a live-in gallery space with a coat of white paint and elbow grease.

headline.main: In Bushwick, a Live-In Gallery That’s an Art Bellwether

docs.lead_paragraph: For the final piece of his performance on Sunday at the Whitney Museum of American Art, Takehisa Kosugi picked up a bow and an electric violin and proceeded to play. It was the last thing I expected him to do at that point, the end of the museum’s two-day retrospective of his work, “Takehisa Kosugi: Music Expanded.” His biography may identify him as a composer, violinist and improviser, but during the weekend’s two shows he had mostly used everyday objects: bicycle spokes, for instance, an inflatable ball, a sheet of paper, or a bag of Japanese soup mix. Some of his compositions unfolded in almost complete silence.

headline.main: Review: In ‘Takehisa Kosugi: Music Expanded,’ Violinist Uses More Than Strings and a Bow

docs.abstract: David Maraniss’s latest book looks back wistfully to Detroit’s heyday in the 1960s, when Motown was rocking and the city was full of promise.
docs.snippet: David Maraniss’s latest book looks back wistfully to Detroit’s heyday in the 1960s, when Motown was rocking and the city was full of promise.
docs.lead_paragraph: Detroit in the early 1960s was a symbol not of urban decline and Rust Belt blight, but of high hopes and youthful dreams. Coveted cars didn’t have model numbers then but names that spoke of flight and fantasy and raw animal power — the Ford Galaxie, Thunderbird and Mustang, the Plymouth Barracuda, the Chevrolet Impala — and they were rolling off the Detroit assembly lines at a record pace. The country was dancing to the beat of Motown’s irresistible pop-soul groove, and with hit after hit by Stevie Wonder, Smokey Robinson, Marvin Gaye, the Temptations and the Four Tops rolling off his assembly line, Berry Gordy would proudly proclaim Motown “the sound of young America.”

headline.main: Review: ‘Once in a Great City’ Chronicles Detroit’s Glory Days

docs.lead_paragraph: Is Jeremy Scott the Donald Trump of American fashion? Not in terms of politics — definitely not in terms of politics — but in terms of positioning? Mr. Scott, after all, is an oft-dismissed polarizing outsider who built his brand beyond the system by mocking fashion’s orthodoxies. He has been categorized as an entertainer and a disrupter, with emphasis on show rather than substance. Yet his approach — Instagram-ready, direct to pop culture consumers — has resulted in a documentary “The People’s Designer”; a stint redesigning the Video Music Awards Moonman statuette, and a second job as creative director of the global brand Moschino. Plus, this week: Mr. Scott’s largest show to date, in front of the singer Rita Ora and the actress Lucy Hale and a chunk of the cast of the TV show “Empire,” including Bryshere Gray.

docs.lead_paragraph: Garth Saloner, the dean of the Stanford Graduate School of Business, announced his resignation on Monday, saying he did not want “a baseless and protracted lawsuit related to a contentious divorce” to hurt the school’s reputation. The divorce involves two Stanford professors. Mr. Saloner began a relationship with the wife shortly after the couple separated, Stanford acknowledged on Monday. The husband is suing the university, saying he was discriminated against. Stanford said he was treated “fairly and equitably.” Mr. Saloner, who has been dean since 2009, told the Stanford community he had become “increasingly concerned that the ongoing litigation and growing media interest will distract all of you.” After Mr. Saloner steps down at the end of the current academic year, he will return to teaching. He did not respond to a request for an interview. U.S. News & World Report rated Stanford’s business school the best in the nation last spring.

headline.main: Stanford Business School Dean to Resign Over a Lawsuit
headline.print_headline: Stanford Business School Dean to Resign Over a Lawsuit

docs.abstract: A critic returns to her early years among Chicago’s black elite.
docs.snippet: A critic returns to her early years among Chicago’s black elite.
docs.lead_paragraph: The phrase “Black Lives Matter,” which emerged as a rallying cry during a year of frequent deadly showdowns between police officers and unarmed black citizens, has almost always been pointed at whites. It’s a way of saying, Stop discounting us. Stop mowing us down with your hatred, fear and disregard. But “Black Lives Matter” might just as easily have been the mantra of America’s black elite who, as far back as before the abolition of slavery, sought to establish themselves in communities characterized by privilege and extreme class consciousness. Of course for them, the phrase would have been transmitted insularly, from one to another, as a reminder of how much was riding upon their success at not merely performing gentility but also believing in the inviolable dignity that gentility has always been thought to confer. Why? Because believing a thing like that will make you less susceptible to everything America has concocted to turn you right back into chattel.

headline.main: Margo Jefferson’s ‘Negroland: A Memoir’
headline.print_headline: Easier Streets

docs.abstract: The word once conveyed a basic human right, but now countries disagree on who's worthy of refuge.
docs.snippet: The word once conveyed a basic human right, but now countries disagree on who's worthy of refuge.
docs.lead_paragraph: It’s an ancient promise: When outsiders flee to a new place in desperate need, they will not be turned away. The Hebrew Bible speaks of six cities of refuge where someone who caused a death unwittingly would be protected from being killed in revenge. The Greeks allowed slaves who ran away from abusive masters and even some criminals to seek sanctuary in certain temples; ‘‘asylum’’ comes from their word for inviolable. According to legend, Romulus, the founder of Rome, extended asylum to people we would call migrants, choosing a spot between two groves on Capitoline Hill for his city’s temple of asylum. ‘‘A crowd of commoners, both free and enslaved, poured in from the neighboring territories, eager for new conditions,’’ the historian Livy wrote. ‘‘This was the first step towards the strength Romulus envisioned for Rome.’’

headline.main: Who Qualifies for ‘Asylum’?
headline.print_headline: Stateless

docs.abstract: Chefs all across the country are redefining the smoked meat plate.
docs.snippet: Chefs all across the country are redefining the smoked meat plate.
docs.lead_paragraph: Across the country, chefs are expanding the definition of the traditional meat plate, swapping out fatty pork for the catch of the day. At Cure in Pittsburgh, Justin Severino has reimagined classics like ’nduja (a spreadable spicy pork sausage) with sockeye salmon, and finocchiona (a fennel-seed salami) with swordfish. At Greenpoint Fish & Lobster Co. in Brooklyn and at Seamore’s in Manhattan, diners can smear rich pâtés of smoked bluefish onto crusty bread. Matt Jennings, the owner of Townsman in Boston, delivers a clever spin on mortadella by substituting scallops for pork. And when Norah in West Hollywood opens next month, Angelenos can dig into smoked trout rillettes and shrimp boudin.

headline.main: Bringing Seafood Charcuterie to the Table

docs.lead_paragraph: 8 P.M. (TCM) BREATHLESS (1961) Turner Classic Movies pays tribute to the director Jean-Luc Godard, starting with this New Wave classic about two erratic days in the lives of star-crossed young lovers — Jean-Paul Belmondo, as a French hoodlum on the lam after killing a cop, and Jean Seberg, as an American expatriate newspaper vendor — living in Paris. As sordid as the film is, “and sordid is really a mild word for its pile-up of gross indecencies,” Bosley Crowther wrote in The New York Times, it is no cliché — rather “more a chunk of raw drama, graphically and artfully torn with appropriately ragged edges out of the tough underbelly of modern metropolitan life.” The evening continues with “Pierrot le Fou” (1968), featuring Mr. Belmondo as an unhappily married man who abandons his bourgeois life for a crime spree with an ex-girlfriend (Anna Karina), at 10:15; “Masculin Féminin” (1966), about an aspiring writer (Jean-Pierre Léaud) who becomes involved with a rising pop star (Chantal Goya) and her roommates, at 12:15 a.m.; “Alphaville” (1965), in which a private investigator (Eddie Constantine) is sent to rescue a scientist from a future world ruled by computers, at 2:15; and “A Woman Is a Woman” (1964), about an exotic dancer (Ms. Karina) intent on finding a man to father a child, at 4. (Image: Ms. Seberg and Mr. Belmondo.)

docs.lead_paragraph: Elizabeth Gilbert’s memoir “Eat, Pray, Love” sold 10 million copies and became the kind of cultural touchstone that makes its author famous, wealthy and controversial. To the book’s fans, including Oprah Winfrey and Julia Roberts (who starred in the movie adaptation), Gilbert’s tale of overcoming a bad divorce and deep depression by traveling to Italy, India and Indonesia in search of pleasure, devotion and balance felt like an authentic and moving search for happiness and enlightenment. To her critics, many of whom never even read it, “Eat, Pray, Love” was a cannily constructed narrative with a pat happy ending that preached personal satisfaction as the highest goal, one you could attain by throwing money around, especially in the third world.

docs.abstract: This novel of the Reagan years shows how the 40th president dominated those around him without revealing himself.
docs.snippet: This novel of the Reagan years shows how the 40th president dominated those around him without revealing himself.
docs.lead_paragraph: Readers of “Finale,” Thomas Mallon’s sly and penetrating ninth novel, are well aware that the book’s protagonist, the nation’s 40th president, is destined to be revered as the Republican Party’s patron saint, his very name synonymous with conservative virtue. However, none of the novel’s characters know this in real time. “Finale” takes place primarily in 1986, two years after Ronald Reagan’s final triumphant campaign and two years before he vacates the White House for good. His presidential legacy is on the line, and the events of 1986 — a fateful nuclear arms meeting in Reykjavik with Mikhail Gorbachev and the brewing Iran-contra scandal — threaten to undo it. The sense of foreboding, bordering at times on panic, that pervades this work of historical fiction stands as an arresting contrast to today’s notion of the unassailable Teflon president.

headline.main: ‘Finale,’ by Thomas Mallon

docs.abstract: The ethicists consider whether mistakes made at 18 disqualify someone from an opportunity.
docs.snippet: The ethicists consider whether mistakes made at 18 disqualify someone from an opportunity.
docs.lead_paragraph: At work, we fill a lot of vacant positions through word of mouth. I recently posted a job on my college’s career network and received a résumé from someone in my graduating class. I’ve never met this person, and I know him to have been a diligent student who won a prestigious fellowship during senior year. He would probably be a leading candidate, and by passing his résumé on, I would be implicitly giving my stamp of approval. The problem is that freshman year he sexually harassed and attempted to sexually assault a good friend of mine. A third party intervened before it escalated and brought her to me and another friend. She decided not to take the incident to any authority, and she eventually worked through the experience. The thought of working with the man who brought so much pain to a good friend is hard to swallow, but I do not know what the ethical thing to do is. It is not my story to share, and I do not want to bring the question to my friend for fear of opening old wounds. Am I allowed to share this information with the head of human resources? Can I take an act committed five years ago by somebody I never met and use it to determine his future job status? Is there a way to bring up my discomfort without outing him? NAME WITHHELD

docs.abstract: With the help of A.I., America’s most famous doll tries to fulfill a timeless dream — convincing little girls that she’s a real friend. What will happen if they believe her?
docs.snippet: With the help of A.I., America’s most famous doll tries to fulfill a timeless dream — convincing little girls that she’s a real friend. What will happen if they believe her?
docs.lead_paragraph: It looked like a child’s playroom: toys in cubbies, a little desk for doing homework, a whimsical painting of a tree on the wall. A woman and a girl entered and sat down in plump papasan chairs, facing a low table that was partly covered by a pink tarp. The wall opposite them was mirrored from floor to ceiling, and behind it, unseen in a darkened room, a half-dozen employees of the toy company Mattel sat watching through one-way glass. The girl, who looked about 7, wore a turquoise sweatshirt and had her dark hair pulled back in a ponytail. The woman, a Mattel child-testing specialist named Lindsey Lawson, had sleek dark hair and the singsong voice of a kindergarten teacher. Microphones hidden in the room transmitted what Lawson said next. ‘‘You are going to have a chance to play with a brand-new toy,’’ she told the girl, who leaned forward with her hands on her knees. Removing the pink tarp, Lawson revealed Hello Barbie.

headline.main: Barbie Wants to Get to Know Your Child

docs.lead_paragraph: NEW YORK — To-day [Sept. 16] is a sizzler. The streets in the lower part of Manhattan between the towering skyscrapers of steel and masonry are stifling with the heat reflected from all sides as well as poured down from above. Despite the busy whirring of thousands of electric fans, offices are like stokeholds, and work is subordinated to the effort to keep cool. Café bars and soda-water fountains are besieged by crowds clamoring for cool drinks, and all pretence at correct dress has been given up in the attempt to reduce discomfort. The Herald is continuing its free distribution of ice and will keep it up indefinitely as long as the hot spell lasts. — The New York Herald, European Edition, September 17, 1915

headline.main: 1915: New York Gasps in Heat Wave

docs.abstract: Ms. Brown’s “Black Girl: Linguistic Play” at the Joyce Theater explores black female identity, and Mr. Kosoko’s “#negrophobia” at Gibney Dance considers the fear associated with the black male body.
docs.snippet: Ms. Brown’s “Black Girl: Linguistic Play” at the Joyce Theater explores black female identity, and Mr. Kosoko’s “#negrophobia” at Gibney Dance considers the fear associated with the black male body.
docs.lead_paragraph: In “Between the World and Me,” widely considered one of the most important books of the year, Ta-Nehisi Coates analyzes the physicality of being black in America, and the burden and symbolism of the black body historically and today. Dance, the voice of the body, is in a distinctive position to contribute to this conversation, and that is especially true this week. Beginning on Tuesday, Sept. 22, at the Joyce Theater, Camille A. Brown presents “Black Girl: Linguistic Play,” which explores the broad spectrum of black female identity. Ms. Brown is a sharp storyteller, and here she illuminates her theme with infectious spirit by borrowing from the ritual of childhood games (through Sunday, Sept. 27). Starting on Wednesday, Sept. 23, Jaamil Olawale Kosoko, a Detroit-born Nigerian-American artist based in Brooklyn, brings “#negrophobia” to Gibney Dance, in which he considers the “erotic fear associated with the black male body” through a personal and a social lens (through Saturday, Sept. 26). In very different ways, both elevate, celebrate and complicate the black body. (Joyce Theater, 212-242-0800, joyce.org; Gibney Dance Agnes Varis Performing Arts Center, 646-837-6809, gibneydance.org.)

headline.main: Camille A. Brown and Jaamil Olawale Kosoko Present Meditations on Black Identity
headline.print_headline: Celebrating Black Identity

docs.lead_paragraph: Thanks to the area’s 50-some colleges, Boston has a reputation for hitting the books first, goofing off second. To be sure, venerable institutions like Symphony Hall, the Museum of Fine Arts and Faneuil Hall still anchor the city’s hold on music, art and history. But in recent years, this little big town has emerged from its brainy, introverted shell to offer a livelier mix of cultural offerings, plus an exploding food scene. The Rose Fitzgerald Kennedy Greenway parkland extends from the North End to Chinatown, connecting a new frontier of glass and steel construction known as the Seaport District to downtown. Of course, this is also a sports- and craft beer-obsessed city, meaning you’re never far from a Celtics, Bruins, Patriots or Red Sox fan hoisting a pint for the home team in one of the Hub’s zillion pubs. Go Boston.

And who better to score the show than Kanye’s best friend, Kanye? He debuted a new song alongside the new collection, featuring Ty Dolla Sign and Post Malone.

docs.lead_paragraph: BACH: Keyboard Concertos No. 1 to 7 (BWV 1052-59) Andreas Staier, harpsichord; Freiburg Baroque Orchestra(Harmonia Mundi)Listening to Bach’s concertos in big gulps may not be the best way to savor their myriad delights, but unless you’re a stronger person than I, you’ll have a hard time turning off the first disc of this double set after the opening D-minor Concerto (BWV 1052), with the propulsive flights of its outer movements. Or the second disc, after the opening D-major Concerto (BWV 1054), with its all-too-brief, teeming finale. Better known these days as a fortepianist, Mr. Staier draws endlessly glinting, shifting colors from his harpsichord, a beautiful-sounding 2011 copy of a 17th-century Flemish original. He delineates structure and suggests mood subtly through embellishments, agogic (rhythmic) accents and in several instances an added cadenza. Brilliant and captivating. (James R. Oestreich)

headline.main: Classical Playlist: Bach, Biber, Gottschalk and More

docs.lead_paragraph: Experts have identified a bone fragment from the second of 43 missing students from a rural teachers’ college who disappeared almost a year ago in a case that has rocked Mexico. The government has said that the students were hauled off buses by corrupt local police officers in the southern city of Iguala and handed over to a drug gang, which killed them and cremated the bodies at a nearby dump. But the students have never been found, and only one, Alexander Mora, had been identified from a bone fragment that the authorities said was recovered near the dump. Attorney General Arely Gómez said Wednesday that advanced testing at the Medical University of Innsbruck in Austria had determined that another bone fragment from the site belonged to Jhosivani Guerrero de la Cruz, who was 20 when he disappeared. An outside panel of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights said recently that the physical evidence at the dump did not support the hypothesis that the students were cremated there.

headline.main: Mexico: 2nd Missing Student Identified

docs.abstract: A tale of mystery, adventure, romance and quest, with an oddball detour.
docs.snippet: A tale of mystery, adventure, romance and quest, with an oddball detour.
docs.lead_paragraph: What does it mean to say that a writer has a “take” on a genre? This question has been popping around my mind since I read Patrick deWitt’s new novel, “Undermajordomo Minor,” which is, let’s just say this straight out, quick and funny and thoughtful and moving and super. But what else is it? The book feels like a take on a certain genre — and let’s figure out what the genre is in a minute — but I’m suspicious of that phrasing, a take, which is often used to draw a divisive line. It is said, for instance, that Margaret Atwood does a take on science fiction and therefore is a literary writer instead of a science fiction writer, and then we wonder why there are so few science fiction writers who write as well as Margaret Atwood, while the science fiction writers glare at us and order another round. This is bad. “The Handmaid’s Tale” is science fiction and should not be disqualified as such on the grounds that it has good sentences and makes you think, as does the work of Patrick deWitt. Therefore, “Undermajordomo Minor” is a terrific piece of genre writing, and that’s that.

headline.main: Patrick deWitt’s ‘Undermajordomo Minor’

docs.lead_paragraph: Down a center flight of marble stairs in the front entrance hall of the Art Institute of Chicago, there is a real-life time machine. It bears no resemblance, however, to any such devices from fiction. There are no displacement spheres, quantum-leap accelerators or flux capacitors; it looks nothing like H.G. Wells’s gilded time-sleigh with its gleaming dinner platter, crystal-knobbed control lever and plush velvet driver’s seat. Indeed, this particular time machine doesn’t even have space for passengers, a fact that becomes immediately apparent upon approaching it. There is only a roomful of wide-eyed drifters trying to project themselves, via intensely prolonged gazes, through a series of glass-paned portals, tilting their torsos and craning their necks as if trying to inhabit the miniature worlds beyond.

docs.lead_paragraph: There is good reason to believe that the conventional 2 percent inflation target is too low, even for the United States; the risks of hitting the zero lower bound are clearly much higher than people believed when 2 percent became orthodoxy. But whatever the case for a higher US target, the case is much, much stronger for Europe, which combines Japan-style demography — a shrinking working-age population, making secular stagnation more likely — with adjustment problems that get much harder when inflation is low. It’s important to realize that it matters not at all whether the overall rate is slightly positive or slightly negative; as the IMF says, “lowflation” creates all the problems we associate with deflation, even if the headline number is greater than zero.

docs.lead_paragraph: A French student of physiology in a letter from the front has described the remarkable behavior of a dog which is his companion in the trenches. ‘‘We have,’’ he writes, ‘‘a sheepdog to which we are very much attached. … His affection for us is touching, and the expression in his eyes when he looks at us is indescribable. But what is most surprising is his conduct under fire. Yesterday I took him some bread. … Shells were raining all round us. One projectile shrieked by overhead. The dog retired almost shamefacedly into his kennel. … Curiously enough, when our guns fire he remains indifferent, and he appears able to distinguish between the noise made by shells fired at us and those we fire at the enemy.’’ — The New York Herald, European Edition, September 18, 1915

headline.main: 1915: Dog Knows Enemy Shell Fire

docs.abstract: “Making Place: The Architecture of David Adjaye” will open at the Art Institute of Chicago on Saturday.
docs.snippet: “Making Place: The Architecture of David Adjaye” will open at the Art Institute of Chicago on Saturday.
docs.lead_paragraph: This Saturday, the Art Institute of Chicago will open “Making Place: The Architecture of David Adjaye,” the largest comprehensive survey of the work of the OBE-awarded British architect on the rise, which originated earlier this year at the Haus der Kunst in Munich. Culling from among over 50 projects Adjaye has built around the world, from libraries to private residences, museums, retail spaces and master city plans, “Making Place” highlights the threads and ideas that lead from one project to the next. “David is a fearless architect, an unconventional thinker, and he is committed to rethinking the possibilities of architecture,” says Zoe Ryan of the Art Institute, who co-curated the show alongside Okwui Enwezor, the Haus der Kunst’s director. It was a fruitful collaboration: “Okwui shows us the work through the lens of contemporary art and I am looking at things through the lens of design and architecture,” she explains. The exhibition aims to bring Adjaye’s projects to life through drawings, sketches, models and a film by Oliver Hardt.

headline.main: A Major Exhibition for an Architect on the Rise

docs.abstract: The photographer Walter Chandoha has been documenting feline antics for over 70 years.
docs.snippet: The photographer Walter Chandoha has been documenting feline antics for over 70 years.
docs.lead_paragraph: Walter Chandoha is definitely a cat person. After photographing cats for over 70 years, he says, “Their potential for photography is unlimited. I still come up with a cat picture that is unlike any cat picture ever made — mine or any other photographer’s.” This fall, Aperture will release “Walter Chandoha: The Cat Photographer,” a collection of his cat career highlights. Chandoha’s photographs have appeared in ads for everything from cat food to shoes, in Ladies’ Home Journal and Life magazine. He opted against glamorous cat casting calls, sourcing most of his models from his own family. “The first was Loco, a kitten I picked up in the snow one night coming home from classes at NYU. He ultimately was responsible for my becoming a freelance photographer specializing in cats,” Chandoha says.

headline.main: The Forefather of Cat Pics

docs.lead_paragraph: The New York cabaret debut of Will Swenson at 54 Below on Wednesday evening had one unforgettable moment. Who should join the 41-year-old Broadway singer (“Les Misérables,” “Lestat,” “Priscilla Queen of the Desert,” “110 in the Shade”) onstage but his wife, Audra McDonald? Together they delivered a tough, combative rendition of “You Don’t Bring Me Flowers,” devoid of the usual sadder-but-wiser sentimentality. As they faced one another and hurled accusations, Ms. McDonald’s eyes flashed with mock fury, and the fight culminated with her slapping him across in the face. The audience erupted with delight.

docs.lead_paragraph: Hummingbirds have an ancient charisma that borders on the mythological. Humble in size, they are endowed with miraculous flying abilities vastly disproportionate to their three-inch wingspans. The birds shimmer like airborne emeralds, and with wings rendered nearly invisible at more than 70 strokes per second, they seem suspended in midair by otherworldly forces. Like fireflies, foxes, bats and toads, they inhabit both the corners of our gardens and our imaginations.

docs.lead_paragraph: The key to James Lecesne’s Sunday, or any day, is chanting. Mr. Lecesne, an actor, writer and activist, has been doing it twice a day since 1993, and he attributes “a certain level of happiness and determination no matter what’s going on” to it. Soon after he started, in an attempt to “make a difference” during the AIDS crisis, he said, he was offered a job at a nonprofit. This led to his meeting the director Mike Nichols, who was instrumental in producing his first show. “I got on track,” Mr. Lecesne said. He is the founder of the Trevor Project, a suicide prevention network for lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender young people, and the star of a one-man play, “The Absolute Brightness of Leonard Pelkey,” which he wrote. Mr. Lecesne, 60, who is “between dogs,” lives alone in a fourth-floor walk-up in the West Village of Manhattan.

docs.lead_paragraph: Franklin and Eleanor Roosevelt’s Hyde Park home may get more press, but their double townhouse on East 65th Street was the scene of quite a lot of family drama in its own right. In 1905, Franklin’s mother, Sara Delano Roosevelt, gave the joined houses to her only child, Franklin, and his distant cousin and new wife, Eleanor, for Christmas. The recently widowed Sara Roosevelt continued to live at the Neo-Georgian-style edifice at No. 47 while the couple moved into the adjacent No. 49. Mrs. Roosevelt senior also asked the buildings’ architect, Charles E. Platt, to add several doors for easy access into the future president and first lady’s marital confines.

docs.lead_paragraph: 9 P.M. (Starz) FURY (2014) An American tank crew — its leader, Sgt. Don Collier (Brad Pitt), a.k.a. Wardaddy, and his motley crew (Michael Peña, Jon Bernthal, Shia LaBeouf and Logan Lerman) — fights its way across Germany in the spring of 1945 as the Nazis retreat toward Berlin in Hitler’s suicidal last stand. Children are conscripted and uncooperative parents murdered. And while the Allies may have momentum, the Germans still have plenty of tanks, many superior to the Americans’. David Ayer, whose drama is less an epic than a series of tense episodes, “has a way of filming violence that is both intense and matter-of-fact,” A. O. Scott wrote in The New York Times. “Like many other post-‘Saving Private Ryan’ combat movies, this one emphasizes the chaotic immediacy of battle, staking its claim to authenticity on the unflinching depiction of bloodshed: Heads are vaporized by mortar rounds. Limbs are severed by bursts of automatic-rifle fire. Human flesh is charred by flames and shredded by shrapnel. But within this gore-spattered, superficially nihilistic carapace is an old-fashioned platoon picture, a sensitive and superbly acted tale of male bonding under duress.” (Image: Mr. Lerman, left, and Mr. Pitt.)

docs.lead_paragraph: Sketching a likeness for a wanted poster is the easy part, according to Stephen Mancusi, a detective who worked as a forensic artist for the New York Police Department for almost 27 years. Getting a witness to describe the face of a perpetrator is the more difficult and nuanced skill. Start by taking five or six minutes to pencil in the shape of a head of average proportions. A face tends to equal five eye-lengths across, while the width of a mouth is about the distance between pupils. Draw quickly: The movement of graphite on paper can be hypnotic. ‘‘People lose themselves watching,’’ Mancusi says. As they do, they relax and remember.

docs.lead_paragraph: NEW YORK — Mr. Dion Boucicault, the well known actor and dramatic author, died of pneumonia to-night [Sept. 18] at his residence in this city. He had for many years dwelt among us and his genial face and flowing white locks were a familiar feature at every first night. For some time past Mr. Boucicault had conducted a school of dramatic art from which he turned out some of our most promising young actors and actresses. It had been noted within the last two or three years that the veteran was getting a little stiff in his movements, but the cheery voice and jaunty Irish manner never left him to the last. His death will prove a severe shock to the profession, of which during a lifetime he was a leading ornament. — The New York Herald, European Edition, September 19, 1890

docs.abstract: Chrissie Hynde, whose rock ’n’ roll memoir, “Reckless,” is No. 7 on the hardcover nonfiction list, recently said she is not very gender-driven: “A good book is a good book. A good song is a good song.”
docs.snippet: Chrissie Hynde, whose rock ’n’ roll memoir, “Reckless,” is No. 7 on the hardcover nonfiction list, recently said she is not very gender-driven: “A good book is a good book. A good song is a good song.”
docs.lead_paragraph: Female Acts: Chrissie Hynde’s rock ’n’ roll memoir, “Reckless,” about life as the lead singer of the Pretenders, enters the hardcover nonfiction list at No. 7, taking its place in a wave of recent titles from the women of rock: Patti Smith’s “Just Kids,” which won the 2010 National Book Award, spent 46 weeks on the hardcover and paperback lists; Kim Gordon’s “Girl in a Band” logged a month this year; and Jewel’s “Never Broken” has just been released. Books are also on the way from Carrie Brownstein, Sinead O’Connor and others. “This is the era of the female act,” the former Rolling Stone editor (and current president of Blue Rider Press) David Rosenthal told The Washington Post this month. “Maybe that has caused overall a hunger for reading about female artists.” Maybe it has. But Hynde told The Post that gender isn’t a big part of the equation for her. “A good book is a good book. A good song is a good song,” she said. “Let me hear it, let me read it. I’m not very gender-driven.” Hynde grew up in a fairly conservative family in Akron, Ohio, and managed, apparently, to hide the more lurid elements of her rock ’n’ roll lifestyle from her mother and father. “I couldn’t have told this when my parents were alive,” she writes in a brief prologue to the memoir. “I would have had to leave out the bad language and tell a lot of lies about what I’d been doing all that time I was gone.”

headline.main: Inside the List

docs.abstract: Times music critics discuss the jazz artist, who sings original lyrics in several languages that incorporate descriptions of Buddhist religious ceremonies, poetry and dreams.
docs.snippet: Times music critics discuss the jazz artist, who sings original lyrics in several languages that incorporate descriptions of Buddhist religious ceremonies, poetry and dreams.
docs.lead_paragraph: Jen Shyu, whose new album “Songs and Cries of the World” comes out this week, is an improvising singer of great accomplishment who leads a band including some of the best improvising musicians in the United States: the trumpeter Ambrose Akinmusire, the violist Mat Maneri, the bassist Thomas Morgan, the drummer Dan Weiss. But she gets much of her inspiration and source material from far outside jazz. Not from pop or classical music or avant-garde traditions. But from music that she has to travel great distances to learn about, like Southern Taiwanese folk songs; or pansori, the South Korean musical storytelling tradition; or sindhenan, the improvisational singing of Javanese gamelan music. (A lot of the music she’s looking for has something to do with her own background: raised in Illinois, her parents are from Taiwan and East Timor.) She achieves fluency in new languages in order to improvise within them; she studies their narrative traditions in order to write within them.

headline.main: Popcast: Jen Shyu and Musical Inspiration

docs.lead_paragraph: Friendship is a bond that is uniquely defined by the people who exist within it. Unlike relationships such as marriage or parenthood, which have clear timelines and boundaries, friendships have no ceremonial beginning or end, no biological definition. They are not sanctioned by any church, nor recognized officially by any state. This is perhaps why women, historically diminished by the government and burdened by the family, find such fulfillment and power among friends.

docs.abstract: Joyce Carol Oates looks to her childhood and beyond in tracing the roots of her vocation.
docs.snippet: Joyce Carol Oates looks to her childhood and beyond in tracing the roots of her vocation.
docs.lead_paragraph: Joyce Carol Oates is an ambivalent memoirist. In “The Lost Landscape: A Writer’s Coming of Age,” she repeatedly ex­presses her doubts about first-person autobio­graphical writing. For one thing, she’s deeply wary of the confessional voice. For another, she has little faith in the reliability of memory. While she can vouch for the accuracy of “A Widow’s Story,” her 2011 account of the aftermath of her first husband’s death, which she based on contemporaneous journals, she can hardly back up this latest memoir with documentation. No small child, not even a Joyce Carol Oates, could be expected to take notes all day. Yet another problem: The memoirist is obliged to leave things out. “To charges of distortion,” she writes, “I can only say — mea culpa.”

docs.abstract: These stories are narrated by the spirits of animals.
docs.snippet: These stories are narrated by the spirits of animals.
docs.lead_paragraph: Ceridwen Dovey studied social anthropology at Harvard before writing her debut novel, the celebrated “Blood Kin” (2007). She continued her studies at New York University afterward, and has now brought an anthropologist’s eye to her second book, the story collection “Only the Animals.” Her subject is not human societies, however, but the relationship between humans and other species. And why not? As J.M. Coetzee says in one of Dovey’s epigraphs, “Each creature is key to all other creatures.”

docs.lead_paragraph: The haunting jacket of Matt Bell’s memorable second novel, “Scrapper,” features the skeletal silos and shafts of a factory through the broken windows of the Fisher Body Plant No. 21, not far from the cloverleaf interchange of I-75 and I-94 in Detroit. Like many locations in the city, this decaying site contains a multitude of histories: Built in 1919, it originally manufactured Buick and Cadillac bodies; during World War II, it produced parts for bombers, tanks and other military equipment; at one point, the factory held a soup kitchen and homeless shelter. Today it stands vacant, most of its metal innards stripped by scrappers, and the monolithic structure is deemed contaminated by the Environmental Protection Agency.

docs.lead_paragraph: About a year ago, I came across “The Life-Changing Magic of Tidying Up” by Marie Kondo on a bookstore table, and because I like to read about organization (more than I like to get organized, really) I bought it, only to toss is aside in frustration a few pages in. I was supposed to clean up all at once, not one room at a time? Pull out every article of clothing, even my carefully stored summer things? And focus on my own mess, not my messy family? This was not helpful. It was impossible, and it made me feel almost as bad as the clutter that still surrounded us.

In tailored jackets, knee socks and button-down shirts, Thom Browne’s schoolgirls were much more prim — though with a wacky twist — as they filed into a schoolhouse before their headmistress. docs.lead_paragraph: The first time that a red carpet was rolled out may have been in “The Oresteia” when Clytemnestra orders her handmaidens to lay down crimson tapestries for the return of her long-absent husband, Agamemnon. The color evokes the blood that was spilled at Troy and signals the blood that will pour from Agamemnon when he’s killed by Clytemnestra, who holds him responsible the death of their daughter, Iphigenia. The red carpet has long held significantly different meanings, although given its grip on the movie world I have started to see it too as a river of blood, cascading from all the footsore celebrities, anxious festival programmers and weary journalists now on that death march called the awards season.

Donatella Versace’s color-block dresses in acid-bright shades were shown with color-coordinated thigh-high boots: very Modesty Blaise. Louis Vuitton and Calvin Klein showed minis with keyhole cutouts, as Jonathan Saunders and Jeremy Scott reverted to trippy retro patterns. docs.snippet: A commission’s worthy recommendations will need strong support lest they slip into the sorry archive of might-have-beens.
docs.lead_paragraph: The track record of “riot commissions” convened after major public disturbances is that they gather dust once they assure the public that something vaguely positive seems to be happening. To its credit, the commission of community leaders appointed to look into the volatile racial protests that rocked Ferguson, Mo., last year did not make that mistake. The 198-page report issued by the Ferguson Commission this week warns from its very first pages that palliatives won’t do this time: Leaders must enact a raft of urgently needed changes, or St. Louis and its ring of disjointed suburbs will never get beyond the deeply troubling mix of racial prejudices and government abuses laid bare in Ferguson.

headline.main: Turn the Ferguson Moment Into Lasting Change

docs.abstract: From the International Herald Tribune archives: The capital of Lithuania is taken by the German army in 1915.
docs.snippet: From the International Herald Tribune archives: The capital of Lithuania is taken by the German army in 1915.
docs.lead_paragraph: Vilna, capital of the Government of that name and the biggest city of Lithuania, has been occupied by the Germans. Details of the city’s fall have not yet been made known, but there is every reason to suppose that the Russian army of occupation has withdrawn intact. For the last few days, as the HERALD indicated yesterday, the fate of Vilna had been in the balance. The enemy occupying Molodetchno and Vidsy, Vilna was practically cut off from all railway communication, and its evacuation, generally regarded as imminent, had doubtless been fully prepared for by the Russian high command. The fall of Vilna, says the “Times” Petrograd correspondent, will facilitate a further German advance along the northern routes and will increase Russia’s difficulties in the matter of transport, both of men and munitions. No official Russian statement has yet been issued, but even the German newspapers do not suggest that the army defending Vilna has been captured. Its escape may therefore be taken for granted, but its position is still a somewhat dangerous one, for an important enemy force threatens its flank from the east. — The New York Herald, European Edition, September 21, 1915

headline.main: 1915: German Armies Occupy Vilna

docs.abstract: Made of radiant silver with a softly hammered surface, it’s part graceful scalpel, part elegant spork.
docs.snippet: Made of radiant silver with a softly hammered surface, it’s part graceful scalpel, part elegant spork.
docs.lead_paragraph: A wedge of cantaloupe, its sweetness intensified by savory paper-thin prosciutto, is a sophisticated dish worthy of its own superlative utensils. The legendary Danish design house Georg Jensen rises to the challenge with this exquisite melon set made of radiant silver with a softly hammered surface — part graceful scalpel, part elegant spork. With furled leaves, tapered endpoints and handles like Ionic columns, the pattern represents the bridge between the house’s Art Nouveau roots and its embrace of Modernism. Out of production for decades, this set is part of a limited edition of reissued pieces, each crafted for luxuriously specialized tasks, from the Acorn collection created in 1915 by the designer Johan Rohde. Also on offer are a dainty grapefruit spoon and a new champagne saber, a Napoleonic-era tool that opens a bottle with one sharp blow to the neck.

headline.main: A Fancy Melon Set, Reissued

docs.lead_paragraph: Chameleons have five digits, but in each hand and foot, these digits are split into two “bundles.” The arrangement permits them to grasp branches and climb with ease, excellent adaptations for life in the trees. A new study reports that the angle between the “bundles” in the tree-dwelling species depends on a large number of previously unknown skeletal elements in the wrist and ankle that fuse together as the embryonic chameleon develops. The fusion produces a ball-and-socket joint that chameleons can use to rotate their bodies while reaching for branches. The study appears in the journal BMC Evolutionary Biology.

docs.lead_paragraph: The former president of a peanut company was sentenced Monday to 28 years in prison for his role in a salmonella outbreak that killed nine people and sickened more than 700 others. The executive, Stewart Parnell, 61, was sentenced about a year after a Federal District Court jury in Albany convicted him of dozens of counts, including introduction of adulterated food into interstate commerce with intent to defraud or mislead. Prosecutors said Mr. Parnell’s company, Peanut Corporation of America, repeatedly sold contaminated peanut products and misled customers about test results. They also said the company, which was headquartered in Virginia but also had facilities in Texas and Georgia, sometimes shipped products that Mr. Parnell knew were tainted. The company filed for bankruptcy and no longer operates. The prison term fell far short of the 803 years that Mr. Parnell faced under sentencing guidelines. He plans to appeal his convictions.

headline.main: Georgia: 28-Year Sentence in Tainted Peanut Case

docs.abstract: Four people — two Canadian men, a Norwegian man and a Filipino woman — were abducted on Monday night from a resort on the southern Philippine island of Mindanao.
docs.snippet: Four people — two Canadian men, a Norwegian man and a Filipino woman — were abducted on Monday night from a resort on the southern Philippine island of Mindanao.
docs.lead_paragraph: Four people — two Canadian men, a Norwegian man and a Filipino woman — were abducted on Monday night from a resort on the southern Philippine island of Mindanao, the police said Tuesday. The victims were identified as John Ridsdel and Robert Hall, both of Canada, and Kjartan Sekkingstad of Norway. The identity of the Filipino woman has not yet been confirmed. The four were taken from the Oceanview Resort on Samal island, off the southern coast of Mindanao, about 11:40 p.m. Mindanao has been a frequent site of kidnappings and violence between government troops and several rebel groups, including Muslim extremists that have pledged allegiance to the Islamic State. But Monday’s kidnapping is the first abduction of foreign tourists in Mindanao in more than two years. In 2012, a Swiss national, Lorenzo Vinciguerra, and Ewold Horn, from the Netherlands, were abducted while bird watching off the coast of Mindanao. Mr. Vinciguerra escaped last December. Mr. Horn is still being held.

headline.main: Philippines: Gunmen Abduct Foreigners
headline.print_headline: Asia; Philippines: Gunmen Abduct 4 People, Including 3 Foreigners, From Resort

docs.lead_paragraph: Both Rob Johnson and Peter Temin direct me to a paper by Gerald Epstein and Thomas Ferguson on the Fed’s strange, destructive turn away from expansionary policy in 1932. They look carefully at the archival evidence, and find that a key factor was the complaints of commercial banks that low interest rates on government securities were squeezing their profits. That is, the turn to tight money in the face of deflation and a collapsing real economy was driven by the same narrow banker interests I have suggested explain current demands for higher rates despite low inflation.

headline.main: Rate Rage in 1932

docs.abstract: The Wisconsin union-slayer drops out early.
docs.snippet: The Wisconsin union-slayer drops out early.
docs.lead_paragraph: About four hours passed yesterday between my hitting “publish” on a post suggesting that Scott Walker’s donors and supporters shouldn’t bail on him just yet and Walker surprising many of those same donors and supporters, as well as the political press, by deciding to drop out of the presidential race entirely. I was obviously among the surprised, and the sheer speed of Walker’s exit makes me think that all the savvy post-mortems might end up missing a key truth: Running for president is hard, unpleasant work, Walker had fought three intense campaigns in just four years, and it’s possible that he simply burned out on running for office sometime in the last two months.

headline.main: Exit Walker

docs.abstract: The last glamorous thing about flying commercial.
docs.snippet: The last glamorous thing about flying commercial.
docs.lead_paragraph: In an airport, there is not much to do but wait, and watch. Our fellow passengers tend to dress as if planning to attend a pajama party at 35,000 feet, of course, while the professionals dress professionally. Amid the terminal boredom, we find ourselves comforted by a pilot’s winged badge, oddly transfixed by a gate agent’s epaulets and charmed by what may be the last remaining glamorous thing about flying commercial, which is the scarf worn by the woman pleading for laggards to fold up their tray tables. While not all female flight attendants wear scarves, the attitude exemplified by Air Canada’s uniform guide — ”Wear your scarf at all times!” — is common enough to keep the item tightly knotted to the iconography of the job. In a traveler’s wishful moments, the panache of the scarf can perk up a slog of a trip with the hint of a colorful jaunt.

headline.main: The Understated Elegance of the Airline Scarf

docs.lead_paragraph: Black Barn Whitewashed barn board walls, steel paneling and an elaborate overhead maze of raw crisscrossed beams give new personality to the space that was the restaurant SD26. “Can you believe it?” asked the chef and owner John Doherty, pointing out the dramatic ceiling. The design, by Mark Zeff, who is also a partner, includes tables for larger parties in roomy alcoves and a chef’s table stationed to one side of the bright open kitchen. The resolutely farm-to-table menu executed by the chef, Matteo Bergamini, who was at SD26, only hints at Italy with an array of charcuterie, a black fig pizza, and porchetta with broccoli rabe. Mushroom toast, lobster salad and grilled corn salad are on the savory side of the menu. Sweets include an apple pudding with buckwheat croutons. There’s a long list of sparkling wines and Champagnes, some served at the compact oyster bar near the entrance: 19 East 26th Street, 212-265-5959, blackbarnrestaurant.com.

headline.main: Black Barn Takes Its Inspiration From the Farm

docs.lead_paragraph: Samu-Jussi Koski, the founder and head designer of the Helsinki-based fashion brand Samuji and its housewares line, Samuji Koti, cites nature as “a huge inspiration.” Hearing him describe the Greek landscape, it’s clear that phrase isn’t just a Q&A cop-out — he finds real motivation in, as he puts it, “the colors of the plants, the hills, the strange flowers, the ever-changing tone of the sky.” On the island Serifos, which he and his husband have visited each summer for the last decade or so, Koski likes to climb to the top of the highest hill at the edge of Chora, reaching a small church at either sunrise or sunset. “The sky that drops to the calm Mediterranean Sea at those times is something so beautiful,” he says. “One cannot find those colors anywhere else.”

docs.abstract: The Wisconsin governor understood the importance of a campaign message, but underestimated the importance of everything else.
docs.snippet: The Wisconsin governor understood the importance of a campaign message, but underestimated the importance of everything else.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Internet is not wanting for explanations of the flameout of Gov. Scott Walker’s short and surprisingly anemic presidential campaign. Walker couldn’t lock down the Republican Party’s conservative base. His average-Joe persona was no match for the scene-stealing Donald Trump. He didn’t understand foreign policy. He didn’t understand domestic policy. He flip-flopped. He was too timid in the first debate. He was too gimmicky in the second debate. Above all, the Wisconsin governor’s downfall illustrates yet again how difficult and unforgiving the business of presidential campaigning is, even for a career politician like Walker.

headline.main: What Scott Walker Could Have Learned From George W. Bush

docs.abstract: “Unfinished Business” is the outgrowth of a much-discussed article for The Atlantic about the difficulty of career advancement for professional women with children.
docs.snippet: “Unfinished Business” is the outgrowth of a much-discussed article for The Atlantic about the difficulty of career advancement for professional women with children.
docs.lead_paragraph: Three years ago, Anne-Marie Slaughter wrote an article for The Atlantic about the difficulty of career advancement for professional women with children. “Why Women Still Can’t Have It All,” which has now grown into “Unfinished Business,” electrified readers. Slaughter’s criticisms of workplace policies and attitudes were not new, but her article had the force of her own belated awakening to the problem. A law professor, author and ­Princeton University dean (now president of the nonpartisan think tank New America), Slaughter had just spent two years as director of policy planning in the State Department under Hillary Clinton — a “dream job” that she initially hoped would lead to further advancement within the agency. But after two years of punishing work hours and a weekly commute between Washington and Princeton, where her husband was taking care of their two sons, Slaughter was surprised to find herself declining more State Department stints. Sometimes a job just couldn’t be squared with family responsibilities, she concluded. She returned to her full-time academic post at Princeton, which offered flexible hours more conducive to family life, and was more or less satisfied with her decision.

headline.main: Anne-Marie Slaughter’s ‘Unfinished Business’
headline.print_headline: Work to Be Done

docs.lead_paragraph: The world of “The Heart Goes Last” starts out feeling familiarly post-­apocalyptic: a destitute married couple, Charmaine and Stan, drift across a devastated landscape, forced to sleep in their car as roving bandits threaten attack each night. As the story expands, we see the novel’s reality is even more disturbing: This is not a different universe, just a slightly exaggerated version of our own. A world where the working class has been pushed off the edge of the economic cliff, and the middle-class dream is alive only as a living nightmare. One of the last sustainable industries is the prison system. “Prisons used to be about punishment, and then reform and penitence, and then keeping dangerous offenders inside. Then, for quite a few decades, they were about crowd control — penning up the young, aggressive, marginalized guys to keep them off the streets. And then, when they started to be run as private businesses, they were about the profit margins for the prepackaged jail-meal suppliers and the hired guards and so forth.”

docs.lead_paragraph: PARIS — The French Communist Party ended 17 years of political isolation today [Sept. 23] by endorsing the leftist presidential candidacy of François Mitterrand. The choice was necessary because a purely Communist candidacy against President Charles de Gaulle might have produced as little as half of its traditional 20 percent of the vote. With Communist, Socialist, and other leftist backing, Mr. Mitterrand can expect 5 to 6 million votes from an electorate of nearly 28 million. He has a good chance of getting more votes than any other candidate except Gen. de Gaulle in the Dec. 5 election. — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, September 24, 1965

docs.abstract: Discover the multiple personalities of the Right Bank, from its most intimate streets to its monumental boulevards and open spaces.
docs.snippet: Discover the multiple personalities of the Right Bank, from its most intimate streets to its monumental boulevards and open spaces.
docs.lead_paragraph: Think Left Bank, and the Latin Quarter and the Eiffel Tower spring to mind. The Right Bank, which is twice the size, has no clear identity. There are, in fact, many Right Banks. There is the Old Regime Right Bank, both monumental and orderly, with some of the city’s best-known sites — the Louvre, the Tuileries Gardens and the Palais Royal. There is the intimate, disorderly Marais, and the elegant open spaces of the revolutionary Right Bank (with the Bastille and Place de la Concorde, where Louis XVI, Marie Antoinette and Robespierre were guillotined). And there is the 19th-century financial Right Bank with its grand boulevards, covered arcades and department stores. Meanwhile, Right Bank villages like Montmartre, Passy and Belleville that were added to the city only in 1860 have struggled ever since to hold on to their local identities. Below is a selection of places that will let you discover the Right Bank’s multiple personalities.

headline.main: 36 Hours in Paris, Right Bank

docs.lead_paragraph: IN Oxford in the 1980s, the covered market in the town center was a warren of small shops, selling everything from antiques to fruit and vegetables. There was an upstairs cafe and a butcher shop that displayed its wares in traditional fashion: Rows of carcasses hung above the entrance and across the front, so that in season it was almost comically festooned with dead game birds. Trays of trotters, liver and other kinds of offal completed the carnivorous tableau, usually arranged artfully around an obscenely grinning pig’s head.

docs.snippet: The experimental pop artist recommends “Andrei Rublev,” Route 395, Frank O’Hara and more.
docs.lead_paragraph: On paper, one could be forgiven for mistaking the music of the experimental pop singer Julia Holter for a particularly eclectic college syllabus. Over the course of Holter’s four albums, she’s taken inspiration from Euripides’s “Hippolytus” (her album “Tragedy”) and Frank O’Hara’s “Having a Coke With You” (her song “Moni Mon Ami”). On her last album, “Loud City Song,” Holter filtered contemporary celebrity through the lens of “Gigi,” a 1958 musical set in turn-of-the-century Paris, based on a novella by Colette. On her new record, “Have You in My Wilderness” (out Sept. 25 on Domino), however, Holter’s inspirations are less thematically unified — more free form — than in the past. “This record is less identifiable with influences,” she says. “It’s not that I don’t use a bit from books or legends or whatever, but each song is different; it’s not like I had loosely based the album on some kind of narrative.”

headline.main: The Art, Drinks, Roads and Poems that Inspire Julia Holter

docs.lead_paragraph: Thomas Mallon’s latest historical novel, “Finale,” picks up effortlessly from his last. And “Watergate” (2012) is a tough act to follow. It’s a shockingly glamorous immersion in the Washington of the Nixon years, with a vast array of characters and a beautifully oblique way of maneuvering them. It makes no difference what knowledge of the Nixon presidency you bring to this marvel of a book. Mr. Mallon has found surprising perspectives from which to look at it and a way of siphoning emphasis away from the turf already trampled by historians. docs.snippet: This Peter Martins production of the Tchaikovsky ballet opened New York City Ballet’s fall season.
docs.lead_paragraph: Sara Mearns, leading the first of four casts of “Swan Lake” and opening New York City Ballet’s four-week fall season at the David H. Koch Theater on Tuesday, has moved light years beyond the melodramatic clichés with which this ballet is usually saddled. The foolish “Black Swan” notion of this ballet makes Odette the good, passive victim and Odile the actively evil demon, while Prince Siegfried looks like a moron for thinking one could be the other. Ms. Mearns, however, interpreting the double role with completely authoritative individuality, makes both heroines arrestingly multilayered. Her Odette reveals a capacity for voluptuous passion within doomed captivity; her Odile is extraordinarily cool, enigmatic, even poignant, notwithstanding sweeping brilliance.

headline.main: Review: ‘Swan Lake’ Features an Authoritative Sara Mearns
headline.print_headline: Imbuing Two Heroines With an Authoritative Air

docs.abstract: The justices should tell us more about why they pick the cases they choose to hear.
docs.snippet: The justices should tell us more about why they pick the cases they choose to hear.
docs.lead_paragraph: Stanford, Calif. — ON Monday, the Supreme Court will meet in private to perform one of its most consequential — yet least appreciated — functions: choosing the cases it will hear. The court’s nine justices hold regular conferences from late September to late June to perform this task. From the roughly 8,000 petitions that arrive at the court each year, the justices select about 75 cases. If four or more justices vote to take a case, it is added to the docket; otherwise, review is denied. Either way, an explanation for the court’s decision is almost never given, nor is it customary to indicate how the individual justices voted.

headline.main: The Supreme Court’s Secret Power

docs.snippet: From the International Herald Tribune archives: Partial prohibition forces France to get creative in 1940.
docs.lead_paragraph: PARIS (via Berlin) — A bootleg and speakeasy industry that flourished in the United States during the dry era has made its appearance in France with the enforcement of partial prohibition. The new law throws a dry blanket on one of the gayest French customs — the aperitif hour. It fixes the alcoholic content of all drinks classed as aperitifs at not more than 16 per cent. The favourite dodge to get a drink of barred liquor is to enter a bar or cafe where you are known and order an ‘‘infusion,’’ which is the French word for herb tea. The bootleg drink is then served in a teacup. — New York Herald Tribune, European Edition, September 25, 1940

headline.main: 1940: Sipping Aperitif From a Teacup

docs.abstract: This week, the California brand Stüssy releases a special collaboration with the Swedish shop Très Bien.
docs.snippet: This week, the California brand Stüssy releases a special collaboration with the Swedish shop Très Bien.
docs.lead_paragraph: For most kids growing up in the 1980s and ’90s, Stüssy was a beloved skater brand — the epitome of California cool. “For our generation, Stüssy, together with other U.S. brands like Nike, Levi’s and Champion, was the uniform at a certain age,” says Hannes Hogeman, who, along with his brother Simon, runs Très Bien, a Swedish store that sells men’s high fashion and streetwear. This Friday, the retailer will launch the Stüssy Très Bien collection, a special collaboration that offers, in the words of Hannes, a more “minimalistic take on street- and sportswear.” There are boxy T-shirts, oversize shorts and a coach jacket with the towns “Laguna” and “Malmö” written on the back (the hometowns of Shawn Stüssy and the Hogeman brothers in California and Sweden, respectively). The collection feels like Stüssy at heart — it features skater-inspired styles with a tinge of Scandinavian refinement thrown in. “The designs came effortlessly, to be honest,” Hannes says. “It was more about removing details, changing the cuts and adding some fabrics that you may not usually get from Stüssy.”

headline.main: A Cult Streetwear Brand Gets a Sleek Update

docs.abstract: The problem with smartphones isn’t their ubiquity. It’s their opacity.
docs.snippet: The problem with smartphones isn’t their ubiquity. It’s their opacity.
docs.lead_paragraph: My mother’s address book is one of the small visual details of my childhood that I can perfectly conjure, although I am sure no photograph of it exists. Fake-leather-bound, filled with her formal, spidery script, it was, to me, barely legible, with addresses crossed out and replaced with new ones as friends’ lives shifted. I often was dispatched to grab it for her from a kitchen drawer. I knew when she was looking for someone’s phone number, which seems unremarkable, except that my own children do not know when I am searching for a phone number, because all they see is me, on my iPhone, intently focused on something mysterious and decidedly not them.

headline.main: Motherhood, Screened Off

docs.abstract: “Space Age,” at Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac Pantin, collects 30 works, some newly commissioned, on the topic spanning five decades.
docs.snippet: “Space Age,” at Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac Pantin, collects 30 works, some newly commissioned, on the topic spanning five decades.
docs.lead_paragraph: Since space exploration has only existed for some 60 years, any artist working before 1950 would be unfamiliar with the visual vocabulary of rockets, shuttles and astronauts. So it follows that “Space Age,” the latest group show at Galerie Thaddaeus Ropac in Pantin, northeast of central Paris, is resolutely contemporary. The show’s 30 works, some newly commissioned, span five decades and offer a vast range of depictions, from a standing diptych by Robert Longo in which the Russian astronaut Valentina Tereshkova (the first woman in space) faces a starry abyss, to a duo of James Rosenquist canvases covered in galactic brightly colored geometries. The newer of his fractal works features a rotating mirror bordered with the words “an intrinsic existence”: selfie or self-reflection, take your pick. Whereas Not Vital’s stainless steel moon sucks viewers into its cratered, spherical surface, Lee Bull engulfs her suspended debris in fog.

headline.main: In a New Group Show, Artists Look to the Sky
